By September 23, soil saturation in Petén, Huehuetenango, Quiché, Alta Verapaz, Izabal, Zacapa, El Progreso, Chiquimula, and Jalapa reached or exceeded 90% in the upper layer, increasing landslide and collapse risks in mountainous areas. Agua Consulta forecasts continued heavy rains in October, with severe flooding reported in areas like the Anillo Periférico, Roosevelt Avenue, and Raúl Aguilar Batres Avenue, disrupting traffic. Insivumeh’s César George predicts the rainy season may end between October 15 and 25 but warns of possible national-scale precipitation systems. The Northern Transversal Strip and Caribbean regions will remain prone to rain. NOAA is monitoring a low-pressure system south of Mexico, which could develop into a tropical depression by week’s end and trigger disordered rains and thunderstorms in central and southern Guatemala. Bardales warns that with about 25 days of rain already recorded since September, further damage from floods, landslides, and mudslides is likely. He attributes this to climate variability and suggests the season could extend into early November, as in 2020 when hurricanes Eta and Iota caused fatalities and disasters. Insivumeh’s October outlook indicates neutral conditions, but there is a 60% chance of La Niña, a 39% chance of neutral conditions, and a 1% chance of El Niño. La Niña typically brings drier conditions in some areas and increased Atlantic hurricane activity. Cold fronts are expected to begin in late October, marking the start of the cold season, which may last until March or April in some regions, with up to 16 cold fronts forecasted, especially impacting the central highlands and western Guatemala.
